subject: biology

items.q: A plant has grown to the normal height for its age, but its leaves have turned yellow. What is the most likely cause?
items.correct: A lack of magnesium ions, needed to make chlorophyll
items.misconception: A lack of nitrate ions, needed to make chlorophyll
items.why: Nitrate is the ion students meet most often, and they associate it with healthy green plants, so any loss of leaf colour is blamed on it. Knowledge of ions is limited to nitrate ions needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth, and magnesium ions needed to make chlorophyll. Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth; magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis.
items.random_wrong: An infection by black spot, a fungal plant disease

items.q: Which of these plant problems is caused by a fungal pathogen?
items.correct: Black spot, giving dark marks on rose leaves
items.misconception: Aphid infestation, giving reduced plant growth
items.why: Aphids are listed alongside viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens as a cause of plant damage, so students assume they must be another kind of microorganism. Plants can be infected by a range of viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens as well as by insects. Knowledge of plant diseases is restricted to tobacco mosaic virus as a viral disease, black spot as a fungal disease and aphids as insects.
items.random_wrong: Chlorosis, giving yellow patches on leaves

items.q: A rose plant has sharp thorns on its stems. Which type of plant defence is this?
items.correct: A mechanical adaptation that deters animals
items.misconception: A physical defence that resists microorganisms
items.why: Thorns and hairs are physical structures you can see and touch, so students file them under 'physical defence' without asking what they act against. Physical defence responses resist invasion of microorganisms: cellulose cell walls; tough waxy cuticle on leaves; layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees) which fall off. Thorns and hairs which deter animals, and leaves which droop or curl when touched, are mechanical adaptations.
items.random_wrong: A chemical defence that kills invading bacteria

items.q: Which of these is a physical defence response that resists invasion of microorganisms?
items.correct: Layers of dead cells around the stems
items.misconception: Poisons which are made in the leaves
items.why: Students treat anything that forms part of the plant body as 'physical', instead of separating defences by whether the plant makes a substance or has a structure. Chemical plant defence responses are antibacterial chemicals and poisons to deter herbivores. Physical defence responses are cellulose cell walls, a tough waxy cuticle on leaves, and layers of dead cells around stems which fall off.
items.random_wrong: Hairs which grow on the leaf surfaces

items.q: A grower sees stunted growth and discoloured leaves on a crop, and a gardening website does not settle what is wrong. What should be done next to identify the cause?
items.correct: Take the plant to a laboratory to identify the pathogen
items.misconception: Add nitrate fertiliser to the soil to restore leaf colour
items.why: Nitrate is the ion students meet most often, and they associate it with healthy green plants, so any loss of leaf colour is blamed on it. Knowledge of ions is limited to nitrate ions needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth, and magnesium ions needed to make chlorophyll. Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth; magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis.
items.random_wrong: Spray the whole crop with a fungicide to kill black spot

items.q: A plant is discoloured and growing poorly. Does this prove a pathogen has infected it?
items.correct: No. Plants can also be damaged by ion deficiency conditions, so the same signs can be produced without any pathogen.
items.misconception: Any damage, discolouration, growth or poor growth seen on a plant means a pathogen has infected it.
items.why: The signs used to detect disease, such as stunted growth and discolouration, are learned as a list of disease signs, so students read every sign as proof of infection. Plants can be infected by a range of viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens as well as by insects, but plants can also be damaged by a range of ion deficiency conditions: stunted growth caused by nitrate deficiency; chlorosis caused by magnesium deficiency.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which type of pathogen causes black spot, and which causes tobacco mosaic virus disease?
items.correct: Black spot is a fungal disease; tobacco mosaic virus is a viral disease.
items.misconception: Black spot is a viral disease and tobacco mosaic virus is a fungal disease.
items.why: Both diseases are met at the same time and both are seen as discoloured marks on leaves, so students swap the two named examples over. Knowledge of plant diseases is restricted to tobacco mosaic virus as a viral disease, black spot as a fungal disease and aphids as insects.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
